title: In your own words
hook: many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray freely and aloud, like talking to a friend

segments.voice: Yesterday, the collect, a one-sentence prayer from 1549. Your line was lighten our darkness. Today's words are made up on the spot.

A Wednesday night in a small church, or a living room. Ten people in a circle. No book. Somebody starts: Lord, thank you for this week. We just bring you Maria's mom. You know what she needs. Then someone else picks it up, and someone else. Plain words, half sentences, a laugh, a long pause. It sounds less like a service and more like a conversation with someone who's in the room. For many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians, this is what prayer mostly is. They'd point to Exodus: "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend." Today closes twelve days on ways to pray, with the simplest one.
screen: `A CIRCLE, NO BOOK.` → `PLAIN WORDS, HALF SENTENCES.` → `AS A MAN SPEAKETH UNTO HIS FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Christians call it free prayer, or extemporaneous prayer: no script, just speaking. It grew strong among the Puritans, then Baptists and Methodists, and later Pentecostals, who wanted prayer to come from the heart as well as the book. Hannah, longing for a child, prays in the temple with her lips moving and no sound, and the priest thinks she's drunk. She tells him she has "poured out my soul before the LORD." A psalm says it plainly: "ye people, pour out your heart before him." All of it: the rent, the kid, the test. And Hebrews says, "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace." The Greek word behind boldly is parresia: speaking freely, holding nothing back. And if you don't know what to say? Paul says the Spirit helps, praying in us with groans that words can't carry. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also pray in tongues, which they understand as a gift of the Spirit; other Christians read those passages differently. Many Christians use both kinds of prayer: set words when their own run out, their own words when the set ones feel far away. Look back on these twelve days and you've met them all: a pattern, a name, a psalm, a slow reading, a look back, an arrow, a list of names, a complaint, a dry spell, a collect. And now, just talk.
screen: `FREE PRAYER: NO SCRIPT.` · `HANNAH POURED OUT HER SOUL.` · `POUR OUT YOUR HEART, BOLDLY.` · `SET WORDS AND YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: Talk out loud for one minute; it may feel strange, but out loud slows you down and makes it real. If you pray, talk to God the way you'd talk to a friend who already knows everything: what happened, what worries you, what you're glad about, in plain words. If you don't pray, say out loud what's on your mind and what you're grateful for, then stop and listen to the quiet.
Parresia, the Greek word for boldness: speaking freely to God without holding anything back, the way you'd talk to a friend.
Your line: just talk. Tomorrow, a new stretch: the circle of the year. Day one hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray aloud in their own words, alone or in small groups, taking turns; many Christians mix this kind of free prayer with set prayers like the Lord's Prayer.
